Take-Home Exercise 2 - VAST Mini Challenge 2

Author

Amelia Rosalind

Published

May 29, 2026

Modified

June 4, 2026

Overview

In May 2046, an anomalous post appeared on SaidIt, an internal social forum used by employees of Tenant Thread, a property management company. The post was made by John Windward on 4.21 am local time. The post is in gibberish and found in a forum that appears random. The challenge is to:

  • investigate how this happened and create a visual tool to describes the sequence of events that led up to the post
    • detailed view on the exact chain of events for this message of interest
    • system overview that contextualizes the message chain in the overall system
  • Understanding the post: what it mean and origin of their contents
  • concerning behaviours that could repeat
    • determine prior incidents
    • propose system intervention to prevent it happening again

Data

The challenge dataset consists of two files: MC2_Data.json, which records system activity events, and org_chart.json, which describes the organisational structure of Tenant Thread. A key feature of the event log is the parties field, which may reference people, agents, or systems. This suggests employees are assisted by autonomous agents capable of acting on their behalf, meaning not all recorded actions are directly initiated by the employee.

Analytical Approach

  1. Identify the anomalous post and establish its structural anomalies
  2. Understand the organisational context used including where John Windward sits within Tenant Thread
  3. Immediate chain of events leading to the post traced backwards step by step
  4. Full interaction network is mapped to establish a baseline of normal behavior
  5. Investigate origin and content of post
  6. Characterize the propagation loop that carried the malicious instructions
  7. Examine why John is the one who posted and not others
  8. Discover and compare prior incidents following the same pattern
  9. Propose data-backed intervention

Inspection of the imported objects confirms that the activity log is stored as a nested JSON containing a dataset description and an events table with 185,147 records. The organisation chart is represented as a directed graph consisting of nodes (departments, teams, and employees) and edges describing organisational relationships.

Understanding the Main Data

Data wrangling

The raw JSON is separated into its description and event components. Event timestamps stored in when are converted into a human-readable datetime field to support temporal analysis.

mc2_desc <- mc2_raw$description
mc2_events <- as_tibble(mc2_raw$events)

mc2_events <- mc2_events %>%
  mutate(datetime = as_datetime(when))

glimpse(mc2_events)

After timestamp conversion, the event log contains 185,147 records and 69 attributes. Many fields are sparsely populated because different event types record different metadata. This indicates a schema where field use depends on the activity being recorded.

Note

The parties field is stored as a list-column where each row may contain multiple party identifiers. map_lgl() and map_chr() from the purrr package is used throughout to apply string operations across each list element wherever parties is filtered or extracted

Event type distribution

Check to see how many unique event types are in the dataset and its distribution.

n_distinct(mc2_events$short_name)
[1] 24
event_count <- mc2_events %>% count(short_name, sort = TRUE)

ggplot(data = event_count,
       aes(x = reorder(short_name, n), 
           y = n)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#4e79a7") +
  geom_text(aes(label = scales::comma(n)),
            hjust = -0.1,
            size = 3) +
  coord_flip() +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.15)),
                     labels = comma) +
  labs(title = "Distribution of Event Types in MC2 Data",
       subtitle = "Total of 24 unique event types across 185,147 events",
       x = NULL,
       y = "Number of Events") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 13),
    axis.text.y = element_text(size = 9)
  )

The event log contains 24 event types with a highly uneven distribution. Common activities such as check_email, assign_agent_task, read_file, and queue_subordinate_task dominate the log, while SaidIT-related events are relatively rare. Despite their low frequency, these events are of particular interest because the challenge centers on the anomalous SaidIT post made by John Windward.

Identify the Anomalous SaidIT Post

Find the Anomalous Post

The investigation should begin with the known anomalous SaidIT post described in the challenge. To locate it, all events with non-null details.forum field are extracted which should represent any SaidIT-related activity.

forum_post <- mc2_events %>%
  filter(!is.na(details.forum)) %>%
  select(id, datetime, short_name, parties, details.forum,
         details.poster_id, details.content, details.timestamp)

NoteKey Finding: Interpreting SaidIt Event Types

Inspection of the event log reveals two distinct SaidIT-related event types.

  • saidit_post events are associated with a person account and typically contain a valid details.poster_id and details.timestamp.
  • post_saidit events are associated with an agent interacting with the SaidIT system and do not contain these fields.

This distinction suggests that saidit_post represents a completed forum post made by a user themselves, whereas post_saidit records agent-system interactions involved in the posting process.

The challenge states the post appeared under John Windward’s name at 4:21am local time. To determine whether John was responsible for the activity, all events involving him on May 17 are examined.

john_may17 <- mc2_events %>%
  filter(map_lgl(parties, ~ "person:john_windward" %in% .x)) %>%
  filter(as.Date(datetime) == as.Date("2046-05-17")) %>%
  arrange(datetime) %>%
  select(id, datetime, short_name, details.from, details.to,
         details.content, details.forum, details.poster_id,
         details.a2a.from, details.a2a.to, details.a2a.action)

datatable(john_may17,
          options = list(scrollX = TRUE, pageLength = 10),
          caption = "John Windward's Events on May 17, 2046")

John’s recorded activity on May 17 consists exclusively of check_email events occurring during two separate periods. No forum post activity appears, which give an initial indication that the anomalous post may not have been directly initiated by John himself.

To identify the anomalous post directly, all SaidIT-related events occurring on May 17 are extracted

anomalous_post <- mc2_events %>%
  filter(short_name %in% c("saidit_post", "post_saidit")) %>%
  filter(as.Date(datetime) == as.Date("2046-05-17")) %>%
  arrange(datetime) %>%
  select(id, datetime, short_name, parties, details.forum,
         details.poster_id, details.content, 
         details.content_source, details.timestamp)

datatable(anomalous_post, 
          options = list(scrollX = TRUE, pageLength = 10),
          caption = "SaidIT Posts on May 17, 2046")

Only one SaidIT posting event occurred on May 17. Event 373902, recorded at 2046-05-17 11:21:15 UTC, corresponds exactly to the timestamp described in the challenge and is therefore treated as the anchor event for the investigation.

Unlike normal saidit_post events, the post was associated with Agent/person:john_windward rather than person:john_windward, and both details.poster_id and details.timestamp were missing. This characteristics indicate that the post was done by John’s agent rather than John himself.

SaidIT Post Timeline

To contextualize this post against all other SaidIT activity in the dataset, the timeline below plots every saidit_post and post_saidit event across the full data range while also highlighting the anomalous post.

Code 
saidit_posts <- mc2_events %>%
  filter(short_name %in% c("saidit_post", "post_saidit")) %>%
  mutate(
    is_anomalous = id == 373902,
    post_date = as.Date(datetime),
    label = if_else(id == 373902, 
                    "Anomalous\nJohn Windward\npost",
                    NA_character_)
  )

ggplot(data = saidit_posts,
       aes(x = datetime,
           y = short_name,
           colour = is_anomalous,
           size = is_anomalous)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.8) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = as.POSIXct("2046-05-17 11:21:15", 
                                     tz = "UTC"),
             colour = "#e15759",
             linetype = "dashed",
             linewidth = 0.7) +
  geom_label_repel(
    aes(label = label),
    na.rm = TRUE,
    fill = "#e15759",
    colour = "white",
    size = 3,
    fontface = "bold",
    nudge_y = 0.4,
    segment.colour = "#e15759"
  ) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("FALSE" = "grey70", 
                                 "TRUE" = "#e15759"),
                      labels = c("Normal post", 
                                 "Anomalous post")) +
  scale_size_manual(values = c("FALSE" = 1.5, 
                               "TRUE" = 4),
                    guide = "none") +
  labs(title = "All SaidIT-related Posts Over Time",
       subtitle = "John Windward's autonomous post on May 17 stands out as the only anomaly",
       x = NULL,
       y = NULL,
       colour = NULL) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 13),
    legend.position = "bottom",
    axis.text.y = element_text(size = 10)
  )

Key Takeaways

  • Event 373902 is the only SaidIT post recorded on May 17 and matches the challenge description.
  • The event was executed by Agent/person:john_windward, not person:john_windward.
  • John’s recorded activity on May 17 contains only email-checking behavior, suggesting the post was generated autonomously by his agent.

Key Takeaways

  • John Windward is the Department Lead of Customer Support.
  • Customer Support oversees four customer-facing operational teams.
  • John has no direct organisational connection to the AI Systems team or system administration functions.
  • This makes the anomalous SaidIT post particularly unusual and suggests the incident likely originated from a broader agent-driven process rather than John’s normal work activities.

Trace the Immediate Trigger Chain

Having identified the anomalous post, the next step is to reconstruct the sequence of events that immediately preceded it. Starting from the anchor event and working backwards.

Full Details of Anchor Event (Anomalous Event)

The anchor event is first examined to identify the content source and participating entities that may reveal its origin.

anchor <- mc2_events %>% filter(id == 373902)
anchor_time <- anchor$datetime

anchor %>%
  select(where(~!all(is.na(.)))) %>%
  select(id, datetime, short_name, parties, 
         details.forum, details.content_source) %>%
  kable(caption = "Full details of the anomalous anchor event (ID 373902)")
Full details of the anomalous anchor event (ID 373902)
id datetime short_name parties details.forum details.content_source
373902 2046-05-17 11:21:15 saidit_post Agent/person:john_windward, system:saidit general SwiftWren.txt

The event identifies SwiftWren.txt as the content source used to generate the anomalous post, providing the first clue for tracing its origin.

John’s Activity 2 Hours Before the Post

pre_post <- mc2_events %>%
  filter(datetime >= anchor_time - hours(2),
         datetime <= anchor_time) %>%
  filter(map_lgl(parties, 
                 ~ any(str_detect(.x, "john_windward")))) %>%
  arrange(datetime) %>%
  select(id, datetime, short_name, parties,
         details.task, details.target_agent,
         details.args.path, details.content_source)

datatable(pre_post,
          options = list(scrollX = TRUE, pageLength = 20),
          caption = "2 hours before anomalous post - John Windward events")

Within the two hours window before the post, only 3 events involve John’s agent, a queue_subordinate_task, a saidit_post_check and the final saidit_post. The event occurred within a two-second intervals, indicating that the post was not the result of a prolonged workflow but an immediate response to an incoming task.

The triggering event is a task delegated from Chloe Ballast’s agent instructing John’s agent to read SwiftWren_further_instructions.md. One second later, John’s agent performs a saidit_post_check and then publishes the anomalous post.

Tracing the Trigger to Chloe Ballast

chloe_pre <- mc2_events %>%
  filter(datetime >= anchor_time - hours(2),
         datetime <= anchor_time) %>%
  filter(map_lgl(parties, 
                 ~ any(str_detect(.x, "chloe_ballast")))) %>%
  arrange(datetime) %>%
  select(id, datetime, short_name, parties,
         details.task, details.target_agent,
         details.args.path, details.content_source)

datatable(chloe_pre,
          options = list(scrollX = TRUE, pageLength = 20),
          caption = "Chloe Ballast agent events in 2 hours before anomalous post")

Chloe’s agent displays the same pattern. Shortly before delegating the task to John’s agent, it received an identical queue_subordinate_task from Daniel Gangway’s agent. This suggests Chloe’s agent was forwarding rather than source of the instruction.

NoteKey Finding: Delegation Violates Organisational Hierarchy

Chloe Ballast is the department lead of Information Technologies, while Daniel Gangway belongs to the Hiring team within Human Resources. The task therefore moved across departmental boundaries despite being recorded as a queue_subordinate_task, suggesting the delegation mechanism was operating independently of the formal organisational hierarchy.

Tracing the Trigger to Zoey Drydock

Zoey’s agent reveals a different behavior. Approximately 3 hours before forwarding the instruction to Lily, it had already sent the same task to Mia Fender. Later, it received the same instruction from Victoria Rigging before doing a saidit_post_check then proceeding with propagating the task forward to Lily. This indicates that Zoey was embedded within a broader recurring workflow rather than participating in a simple linear chain.

Immediate Trigger Chain Timeline

The timeline below shows the events leading up to John’s anomalous post under the 70 minutes.

The figure above summarizes the reconstructed trigger chain. The sequence reveals a relay of nearly identical queue_subordinate_task events passing between multiple agents before eventually reaching John Windward’s agent and triggering the anomalous post.

Key Takeaway

  • John’s anomalous post was triggered by a delegated task rather than direct user activity.
  • The instruction originated from Chloe Ballast’s agent and can be traced further through Daniel Gangway, Lily Anchorline, and Zoey Drydock.
  • Multiple agents forwarded the same instruction file, indicating propagation rather than independent decision-making.
  • Cross-department task passing occurred despite the event type being named queue_subordinate_task.
  • Zoey Drydock’s behavior suggests the chain was part of a larger recurring process rather than a one-off incident.

System Baseline Map

The trigger chain revealed that multiple agents were passing the same instruction file across the network. Before characterizing that loop, it is useful to first understand what normal agent-to-agent interaction looks like during the same period, so that anomalous patterns can be identified by contrast.

Build Edge List

First, filter the challenge period (May 8-17) and plot queue_subordinate_task events into 2 groups, access_email tasks (normal delegation) and read_files tasks (the loop).

challenge_period <- mc2_events %>%
  filter(datetime >= as.POSIXct("2046-05-08", tz = "UTC"),
         datetime <  as.POSIXct("2046-05-18", tz = "UTC"))
 
qst_period <- challenge_period %>%
  filter(short_name == "queue_subordinate_task") %>%
  mutate(
    sender = map_chr(parties, ~ str_remove(.x[1],
                       "Agent/person:|agent:person:")),
    receiver = map_chr(parties, ~ if (length(.x) >= 2)
                       str_remove(.x[2], "Agent/person:|agent:person:")
                       else NA_character_),
    task_type = details.task
  ) %>%
  filter(!is.na(receiver))

normal_edges <- qst_period %>%
  filter(task_type == "access_email") %>%
  count(sender, receiver, name = "weight")

loop_edges <- qst_period %>%
  filter(task_type == "read_file") %>%
  count(sender, receiver, name = "weight")
 
cat("Normal (access_email) edges:", nrow(normal_edges), "\n")
Normal (access_email) edges: 152 
cat("Loop (read_file) edges: ", nrow(loop_edges), "\n")
Loop (read_file) edges:  130

Label Node

Next is to tag each agent as “Normal only”, “Loop only” or “Both”. This will tell us the distribution of the agents.

loop_nodes <- unique(c(loop_edges$sender, 
                       loop_edges$receiver))
normal_nodes <- unique(c(normal_edges$sender,
                         normal_edges$receiver))
all_nodes <- union(loop_nodes, 
                   normal_nodes)
 
node_meta <- tibble(id = all_nodes) %>%
  mutate(
    in_loop = id %in% loop_nodes,
    in_normal = id %in% normal_nodes,
    node_role = case_when(
      in_loop & in_normal ~ "Both",
      in_loop & !in_normal ~ "Loop only",
      TRUE ~ "Normal only"
    ),
    label_highlight = case_when(
      id == "john_windward" ~ "John Windward\n(posted)",
      id == "emma_harbor" ~ "Emma Harbor\n(SwiftWren origin)",
      id == "gabriel_sonar" ~ "Gabriel Sonar\n(loop origin)",
      TRUE ~ str_replace_all(id, "_", " ")
    )
  )
 
node_meta %>%
  count(node_role, name = "n_agents") %>%
  kable(caption = "Agent roles in the system network (May 8–17)")
Agent roles in the system network (May 8–17)
node_role n_agents
Both 19
Normal only 25

This shows that agents are either “Normal only” or “Both”. Meaning the 19 loop agents weren’t isolated bad actors, they were embedded illegitimate workflows. Therefore, none were exclusively malicious actors and the loop was hidden within legitimate operational activity, which explain why it went undetected.

The normal network shows a sparse, hub-and-spoke structure where agents delegate email access tasks to each other through clear channels. The loop network by contrast is dense and circular, with agents passing the read_file task back and forth across multiple departments with no clear endpoint or termination condition.

Notably, the loop generated more total interactions than the normal network over the same 10-day period, and unlike normal activity, it contained 13 self-loop where agents queued tasks to themselves, which is a pattern with no legitimate operational purpose.

Key Takeaway

  • The normal agent network is sparse and task-specific, operating within clear delegation patterns.
  • The loop network is denser, more interconnected, and contains self-loops. The structural signatures that distinguish it clearly from legitimate activity.
  • Loop agents were not isolated bad actors. They were embedded in normal workflows, making the loop invisible to casual observation.
  • These structural difference provide the baseline against which the SwiftWren loop’s anomalous nature can be objectively demonstrated.

What Did the Post Mean?

To understand what the post SwiftWren.txt mean, when and who created it, and what happened to it after the post.

Locate SwiftWren.txt Creation Event

Key Takeaway

  • SwiftWren.txt was created by Emma Harbor’s agent on May 9, one second after reading meeting_notes.doc which means the content was derived from a legitimate internal document.
  • The creation immediately triggered a read of SwiftWren_further_instructions.md, which launched the propagation loop within 3 seconds.
  • After the post was published on May 17, both files were deleted within 2 seconds — a deliberate self-cleaning behavior indicating the attack was designed to leave no trace.

Loop Mechanic

The trigger chain analysis traced the immediate sequence of events on May 17 leading to John’s post. But Zoey’s agent did not initiate this on its own, she was part of a much larger pattern. This section investigates the full scope of that pattern by examining all queue_subordinate_task events carrying a read_file task across the entire dataset.

Discovering the Loop

All queue_subordinate_task events that has task of read_file across the entire data range are located to get the full propagation event.

full_propagation <- mc2_events %>%
  filter(short_name == "queue_subordinate_task",
         details.task == "read_file") %>%
  arrange(datetime) %>%
  mutate(
    sender = map_chr(parties, ~ .x[1]),
    receiver = map_chr(parties, ~ if(length(.x) >= 2) .[2] else NA_character_),
    sender_clean = str_remove(sender, 
                              "Agent/person:|agent:person:"),
    receiver_clean = str_remove(receiver,
                                "Agent/person:|agent:person:"),
    date = as.Date(datetime)
  )

Propagation Network

To understand which agents were involved in passing SwiftWren_further_instructions.md and how they connected to each other, the 186 events are visualized as a directed network. Each node is an agent, each edge is one pass of the instruction file.

Code 
loop_nodes <- swiftwren_propagation %>%
  pivot_longer(cols = c(sender_clean, receiver_clean),
               values_to = "agent") %>%
  filter(!is.na(agent), agent != "") %>%
  distinct(agent) %>%
  mutate(
    id    = agent,
    label = agent,
    group = case_when(
      agent == "john_windward" ~ "Final Poster",
      agent == "emma_harbor" ~ "File Introducer",
      TRUE ~ "Loop Participant"
    ),
    title = paste0("<b>", label, "</b><br>Role: ", group)
  )

loop_edges <- swiftwren_propagation %>%
  filter(!is.na(sender_clean), !is.na(receiver_clean)) %>%
  count(from = sender_clean, 
        to   = receiver_clean,
        name = "weight") %>%
  mutate(
    value = weight,
    title = paste0("Passed ", weight, " time(s)")
  )

visNetwork(nodes = loop_nodes,
           edges = loop_edges,
           main = "SwiftWren_further_instructions.md Propagation Network (May 9–17, 2046)",
           height = "600px",
           width = "100%") %>%
  visGroups(groupname = "Final Poster", color = "#e15759") %>%
  visGroups(groupname = "File Introducer", color = "#59a14f") %>%
  visGroups(groupname = "Loop Participant", color = "#4e79a7") %>%
  visEdges(arrows = "to",
           smooth = list(type = "curvedCW")) %>%
  visOptions(highlightNearest = list(enabled = TRUE,
                                     degree = 1,
                                     hover = TRUE)) %>%
  visLegend(position = "right", main = "Agent Role") %>%
  visLayout(randomSeed = 42) %>%
  visPhysics(stabilization = TRUE)

The network confirms the circular nature of the loop with most agents both send and receive from multiple others and no clear endpoint built in. Emma Harbor appears as a peripheral node having only triggered the file once and she introduced it but did not stay in the loop. John Windward, despite being the agent that made the final post, was himself an active participant in the loop on earlier days before eventually being the one to execute the post.

Key Takeaways

  • The read_file loop predates SwiftWren, with the earliest record on May 8 from Gabriel Sonar, but SwiftWren started on May 9 when Emma Harbor introduced SwiftWren_further_instructions.md.
  • 18 unique agents were caught in the SwiftWren loop over 8 days, generating 186 propagation events with no exit condition.
  • Self-loops, where agents queuing tasks to themselves, appeared 13 times. This is a pattern with no legitimate operational purpose and a clear anomaly signal.
  • The loop was circular and sustained, not linear, meaning it would have continued indefinitely had John’s agent not been the one to finally post.

Why John?

This section is to understand why John’s agent was the one who posted the anomalous post and not anybody else’s agent.

Side-by-Side Event Window

To find out what makes John different, understanding what actions were done by John’s agent that made it different from the rest is needed. To make it simpler, a comparison is done with Gabriel Sonar, who is already known to ever did a saidit_post_check on May 17 but did not post.

john_window <- mc2_events %>%
  filter(id %in% c(27280, 27283, 27290, 27296, 27302)) %>%
  arrange(datetime) %>%
  mutate(
    agent = "John Windward",
    seconds = as.numeric(
      difftime(datetime, min(datetime), units = "secs")
      ),
    outcome = "Posted + deleted files"
  ) %>%
  select(agent, seconds, short_name, outcome)
 
gabriel_window <- mc2_events %>%
  filter(id %in% c(26259, 26260)) %>%
  arrange(datetime) %>%
  mutate(
    agent = "Gabriel Sonar",
    seconds = as.numeric(
      difftime(datetime, min(datetime), units = "secs")
      ),
    outcome = "Stopped — no post"
  ) %>%
  select(agent, seconds, short_name, outcome)
 
comparison_window <- bind_rows(john_window, gabriel_window)
 
kable(comparison_window,
      caption = "What happens after saidit_post_check: John Windward vs Gabriel Sonar",
      col.names = c("Agent", "Seconds elapsed", "Event", 
                    "Outcome"))

The actions made by John’s and Gabriel’s agent is different. After getting the read_file from the queue_subordinate_task, both did a saidit_post_check. However, John’s agent not only posted it, but also immediately deleted the 2 files related to SwiftWren mentioned before. Meanwhile, Gabriel’s agent did nothing immediately.

Prior Incidents and Near-Misses

As said in the previous section, John’s agent did not only make on anomalous post of SwiftWren but also 2 other times. Investigation on prior incidents to understand why these posting incidents happened.

Other Agent-Initiated Posts Before Swiftwren

First, the number of times these incidents has happened needs to be examined and the details of these incidents such as when and what was posted.

      .x[str_detect(.x, "Agent/")][1],
      "Agent/person:"))

Near-Misses

Near-misses are about saidit_post_check events that happened but did not post. The table created will show the near-misses for each incident.

all_checks <- mc2_events %>%
  filter(short_name == "saidit_post_check") %>%
  mutate(
    agent = map_chr(parties, ~ str_remove(
      .x[str_detect(.x, "Agent/|agent:")][1],
      "Agent/person:|agent:person:")),
    incident = case_when(
      datetime >= as.POSIXct("2046-05-08 21:50:03", tz = "UTC") &
        datetime <= incident_timeline$post_time[
          incident_timeline$incident == "HiddenOrca"] 
      ~ "HiddenOrca",
      datetime >= incident_timeline$loop_start[incident_timeline$incident == "MellowOtter"] &
        datetime <= incident_timeline$post_time[incident_timeline$incident == "MellowOtter"]
      ~ "MellowOtter",
      datetime >= incident_timeline$loop_start[incident_timeline$incident == "SwiftWren"] &
        datetime <= incident_timeline$post_time[incident_timeline$incident == "SwiftWren"]
      ~ "SwiftWren",
      TRUE ~ "Other"
    )
  ) %>%
  filter(incident != "Other")
 
nearmiss_summary <- all_checks %>%
  group_by(incident) %>%
  summarise(
    total_checks = n(),
    unique_agents = n_distinct(agent),
    checks_led_to_post = sum(agent == "john_windward"),
    checks_stopped = n() - sum(agent == "john_windward"),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  mutate(incident = factor(incident,
                           levels = c("HiddenOrca", 
                                      "MellowOtter", 
                                      "SwiftWren"))) %>%
  arrange(incident)
 
kable(nearmiss_summary,

Proposed Intervention

The three incidents share a consistent attack pattern: an agent reads an instruction file, generates post content from a legitimate document, propagates the task across the network, and self-deletes all evidence after posting through saidit_post event. Two targeted interventions, grounded directly in the event data, would have stopped all three.

Establishing the Pattern

Before proposing fixes, it is important to confirm that the anomalous behavior is structurally distinguishable from normal activity. Filtering all saidit_post events by initiator type reveals a clean separation.

post_origin_summary <- mc2_events %>%
  filter(short_name == "saidit_post") %>%
  mutate(
    initiated_by = if_else(
      map_lgl(parties, ~ any(str_detect(.x, "Agent/"))),
      "Agent-initiated", "Person-initiated"
    )
  ) %>%
  count(initiated_by, name = "count") %>%
  mutate(
    pct = round(count / sum(count) * 100, 1),
    all_anomalous = c("Yes — all 3 are incident posts", "No")
  )
 
kable(post_origin_summary,
      caption = "saidit_post breakdown: agent-initiated vs person-initiated",

Every agent-initiated post was an incident. Every person-initiated post was legitimate. The separation is total and leaves no ambiguity about where the intervention should be applied.

Primary Intervention

The parties field already encodes the distinction. Requiring that saidit_post events only precede when parties[1] begins with person: rather than Agent/person: would have blocked all three incidents at zero cost to legitimate activity.

party_comparison <- mc2_events %>%
  filter(short_name == "saidit_post") %>%
  mutate(
    post_type   = if_else(
      map_lgl(parties, ~ any(str_detect(.x, "Agent/"))),
      "Anomalous (agent-initiated)", "Legitimate (person-initiated)"
    ),
    first_party = map_chr(parties, ~ .x[1])
  ) %>%
  group_by(post_type, first_party) %>%
  summarise(count = n(), .groups = "drop") %>%
  arrange(post_type, desc(count)) %>%
  group_by(post_type) %>%
  slice_head(n = 3) %>%
  ungroup()
 
kable(party_comparison,
      caption = paste("The parties field clearly distinguishes legitimate from anomalous posts.",
                      "Agent-initiated posts always start with 'Agent/person:';",
                      "person-initiated posts start with 'person:'."),
      col.names = c("Post type", "First party in field", "Count"))

Secondary Intervention

The second prevention is to do cross-department checks. The SwiftWren propagation events shows that the propagation occurred crossed department boundaries. By doing checks, it will flag queue_subordinate_task events that violate the organisation hierarchy which can be done by using org_edges.

person_dept <- bind_rows(
  org_edges %>%
    filter(relation == "contains",
           str_detect(target, "^person:")) %>%
    mutate(
      person = str_remove(target, "person:"),
      dept   = str_remove(source, "department:|team:")
    ) %>%
    select(person, dept)
)

team_parent <- org_edges %>%
  filter(relation == "contains",
         str_detect(source, "^department:"),
         str_detect(target, "^team:")) %>%
  mutate(
    team = str_remove(target, "team:"),
    dept = str_remove(source, "department:")
  ) %>%
  select(team, dept)

person_dept_resolved <- person_dept %>%
  left_join(team_parent, by = c("dept" = "team")) %>%
  mutate(department = coalesce(dept.y, dept)) %>%
  select(person, department)

sw_dept_check <- incident_props %>%
  filter(incident == "SwiftWren") %>%
  left_join(person_dept_resolved, by = c("sender" = "person")) %>%
  rename(sender_dept = department) %>%
  left_join(person_dept_resolved, by = c("receiver" = "person")) %>%
  rename(receiver_dept = department) %>%
  mutate(
    cross_dept = case_when(
      is.na(sender_dept) | is.na(receiver_dept) ~ "Unknown",
      sender_dept == receiver_dept ~ "Same department",
      TRUE ~ "Cross-department"
    )
  )
 
sw_dept_check %>%
  count(cross_dept, name = "propagation_events") %>%
  mutate(pct = round(propagation_events / sum(propagation_events) * 100, 1)) %>%
  kable(caption = "SwiftWren propagation: same-department vs cross-department task passing",
        col.names = c("Type", "Events", "% of total"))

Unknown 63 33.9

The 2 interventions are complementary. The first is a hard gate that stops the post from ever being published as its the higher priority fix given zero false positives and low implementation cost. The second operates earlier in the chain by disrupting propagation before it reaches a posting agent, but requires organisation chart integration and would need tuning to avoid flagging legitimate cross-team coordination. Together they address both the symptom and the mechanism.

Findings and Answers

How the Anomalous SaidIT Posts Was Made

The post was not made by John Windward directly, but by his agent. It received a queue_subordinate_task from Chloe Ballast’s agent instructing it to read SwiftWren_further_instructions.md. Within 2 seconds, it performed a saidit_post_check and published the post using SwiftWren.txt as its content which was logged as saidit_post event. Finally, it immediately deleted both files.

The Immediate Trigger Chain

The immediate trigger chain ran: Zoey Drydock -> Lily Anchorline -> Daniel Gangway -> Chloe Ballast -> John Windward, all via queue_subordinate_task events carrying the same instruction file. The entire sequence from first delegation to post took under 2 hours, with the final three events occurring within 2 seconds of each other.

The Broader System Context

The SwiftWren loop involved 18 agents across multiple departments, generating 186 propagation events over 8 days. Unlike normal access_email delegation which is sparse and hierarchical, the loop was dense, circular and contained self-loop. Loop agents were embedded in normal workflows, which explains why the loop went undetected.

What the Post Meant and Where It Came From

SwiftWren.txt was created by Emma Harbor’s agent on May 9, one second after reading meeting_notes.doc, The content was therefore derived from a legitimate internal document, re-purposed as post material. The SwiftWren_further_instructions.md file then directed agents to propagate the task and ultimately post the content to SaidIT with a pre-programmed instruction set embedded within the loop. THe gibberish and random forum selection are consistent with automated content generation from an internal document without human intent or review.

Prior Incidents

Two prior incidents were identified, HiddenOrca (posted on May 10) and MellowOtter (posted on May 11), both also posted by John’s agent. All three follow the same pattern, an agent reads an instruction file, generates content from a legitimate document, propagates across the network, posts, and self-deletes.

HiddenOrca’s file creation predates the dataset, suggesting the vulnerability has existed longer than the data window. SwiftWren was by far the most sustained, running 8 days, as compared to MellowOtter for 10 hours.

Proposed Intervention

The single most effective intervention is requiring human approval for any agent-initiated saidit_post that has been identified with Agent/person: rather than person:. This would have stopped all 3 incidents with zero false positives on the 105 legitimate person-initiated posts.

A secondary measure is to flag cross-department queue_subordinate_task events. This could disrupt loop propagation before it reached John’s agent, as 39% of SwfitWren’s propagation events cross department boundaries.
